analysis.one_liner: Makes foreign oil cartels like OPEC subject to U.S. antitrust lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee: it was referred there on the day it was introduced in 2005 and died without a vote when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Sherman Antitrust Act to declare it illegal for foreign countries to band together to limit oil and gas production or set prices when those actions affect the U.S. market. It would strip such countries of sovereign immunity — the legal shield that normally keeps foreign governments out of U.S. courts — and let the Attorney General and the Federal Trade Commission sue them. The bill was introduced by Rep. John Conyers and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers and businesses that buy gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products. If lawsuits forced OPEC countries to stop coordinating output cuts and price-setting, oil supplies could increase and pump prices could fall, or the mere threat of litigation could deter price-fixing behavior.

how_it_helps.text: Declares it illegal under the Sherman Act for foreign states to act as a cartel to limit oil production, set petroleum prices, or otherwise restrain trade when those actions have a direct, substantial, and foreseeable effect on the U.S. market.

Removes the sovereign immunity that normally protects foreign governments from being sued in U.S. courts, and overrides the act of state doctrine so courts must decide cases on the merits rather than dismissing them as political questions.
Authorizes the Attorney General and the Federal Trade Commission to bring enforcement actions in federal district court.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign oil-producing states and their national oil companies would face lawsuits, potential judgments, and exposure under U.S. antitrust law. Domestic oil producers could also face lower prices if a dismantled cartel produced more oil. Energy analysts and government officials have long warned that such litigation could provoke retaliation from oil-exporting countries against U.S. interests.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives no private right of action to consumers — only the Attorney General and FTC could sue, so the benefit to individual drivers depends entirely on federal enforcement choices.

Suing sovereign oil states in U.S. courts risks diplomatic and economic retaliation — oil-exporting countries could restrict supply or cut off cooperation with the U.S., which could push prices up rather than down.
Enforcing a U.S. antitrust judgment against foreign governments would be practically difficult, since there is no obvious mechanism to collect from foreign states even after winning in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea addresses a real cost to consumers — a cartel of foreign governments sets the price of a commodity every household buys — but the remedy is blunt and its effectiveness is uncertain. It relies on federal litigation against foreign sovereigns, risks foreign retaliation, and offers no direct private cause of action. Whether it would lower pump prices or simply provoke confrontation is genuinely unclear.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the No Oil Producing and Exporting Cartels Act of 2005 in the House on February 9, 2005.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which was its only committee assignment.
The bill attracted four cosponsors and no further action; the congressional record shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign oil-producing cartels and oil producers generally are better off, since they faced no possibility of U.S. antitrust suits. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's failure, but the loss was modest given the bill's uncertain effectiveness.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: Ranking Member, House Judiciary Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor the day it was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress expired.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has historically opposed antitrust exposure for oil-producing states, arguing litigation against foreign oil nations could trigger retaliation and disrupt energy markets.

sides.party_line_note: The four cosponsors included a Republican, two Democrats, and an Independent, but the bill drew almost no congressional support of either party — only five members total backed it in two years.

industries.note: These states coordinate production limits and pricing, which raises the cost of gasoline, heating fuel, and everything that depends on oil. The bill would make that coordination actionable in U.S. courts.

Breaking a foreign cartel that limits supply could lower world oil prices, reducing domestic producers' revenues — though some domestic firms have also faced OPEC-related pricing dynamics. Their interest runs partly against consumers, who pay the cartel's prices.
